text: Each height at index i is a vertical line. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, hold the most water, and return that maximum area.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the area between lines i and j is the shorter of the two heights times the width, j minus i, since water spills over the lower side. For one, eight, six, two, five, four, eight, three, seven, the answer is forty-nine. Middle lines don't block the water here — only the two I pick matter, right? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Correct — only the two chosen lines matter. n is up to ten to the fifth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every pair — that's n squared, around ten to the tenth for n of ten to the fifth, way too slow. This problem reminds me of converging two pointers with a greedy move. I start at the widest pair, both ends, and walk inward. Width only shrinks as I move in, so the only way to beat the current area is to raise the shorter wall — so each step I move the shorter side inward. That's linear time, constant space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Why is moving the shorter wall safe — couldn't you skip the optimum?

Say the left wall is shorter. Moving it discards every pair of l with some j before r. Each of those is narrower, and still capped by the short left wall, so its area is at most the area I just recorded. None can beat it, so dropping them loses nothing. Moving the taller wall instead keeps the same low cap but shrinks the width — strictly worse, and it might throw away the real optimum. On a tie, either move is safe, by the same argument.

Here's the plan. One: l at zero, r at n minus one, max area zero. Two: each step, compute the shorter height times r minus l, and update the max. Three: if the left height is lower, move l right; otherwise move r left. I compute before moving, so the current pair is never skipped.

Alright, let me code this up. One while loop, as long as l is less than r. Inside, the current area is the min of the two heights times r minus l, and I fold it into max area. Then I move whichever wall is shorter. One thing worth flagging — the comparison is strictly less than, so on a tie the else branch moves r. That's fine: with equal walls, neither end can do better with anything in between. And the area is computed before the move, so the pair I'm standing on always gets counted.

Let's dry-run the code. One, eight, six, two, five, seven — expected twenty-eight. The row that matters is the first move: at the two ends the area is one times five, five, and the height-one wall is shorter, so l moves in. Now eight and seven at width four give twenty-eight in one move — that's the greedy paying off. Every later pair is narrower and smaller, so it returns twenty-eight. That matches. Corner cases: with just two lines, it checks that one pair and stops. If every height is equal, the very first pair, the widest, wins.
Isn't this the same as computing how much rain water a terrain traps?

No — they look alike but differ. Here I pick two walls for one rectangle; the middle lines don't hold water. In the trapping version, every cell holds the min of its left max and right max, minus its own height, and you sum all of it. Max of one rectangle versus sum over all cells.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: l only rises and r only falls, so there are fewer than n steps in total. Space is constant — two indices. Oh, one more thing — if I doubted the greedy under pressure, I'd cross-check it against the n squared brute force on random small arrays. That's cheap insurance for a greedy that's easy to state and harder to prove.
Great — the min-not-max area, the move-shorter proof, compute-before-move, and you kept it distinct from the trapping-water problem. Done.
